strengths: Well-motivated problem identification with compelling empirical evidence (Table 3) that existing metrics miss important forgetting aspects

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 9 unlearning methods, multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, Tiny ImageNet) and architectures (ResNet-18, ViT) with rigorous reporting of results with standard deviations
Clear mathematical definitions of CR and MIACR metrics that directly address identified limitations, with effective motivation via Grad-CAM visualization
General unlearning framework applicable to multiple training-based methods showing consistent improvements while preserving model utility
Thorough experimental analysis revealing that methods performing well on traditional metrics (UA, MIA) do not necessarily achieve strong forgetting under CR metric
weaknesses: Foundational theoretical concern: Exchangeability assumption required by conformal prediction's formal guarantees is acknowledged to not hold in machine unlearning settings but dismissed with a footnote without rigorous justification of why statistical validity is maintained

Arbitrary α (miscoverage rate) selection creates metric instability: default α=0.1 choice lacks principled justification; results are sensitive to α (Table 4 shows method rankings change with α); at α=0.2 many methods yield Set Size < 1, which is problematic

Limited novelty in proposed framework: straightforward replacement of softmax with non-conformity score in C&W loss; modest empirical improvements (3-9% UA gain) with no theoretical analysis of optimality

Significant practical overhead inadequately addressed: requires dual calibration sets (Dc, D'c) doubling data requirements; no computational cost analysis; distribution shift handling (shadow model) adds complexity
Narrow experimental scope limited to image classification only (CIFAR-10, Tiny ImageNet); unclear if findings generalize to NLP, tabular data, or other domains
Incomplete comparison with related work: only compares against UA/MIA; no comparison with other uncertainty quantification methods or recent unlearning evaluation approaches
Technical choices lack justification: margin parameter Δ=0.01 arbitrary; MIACR binary definition (only measuring {0}) seems restrictive; calibration set size analysis limited to single setting
Distribution shift handling (Section B.4) reveals method limitations but relegated to appendix; suggests approach may not gracefully handle certain unlearning strategies like label corruption

strengths: Clear identification of a real problem: existing unlearning metrics don't ensure true label exclusion from prediction sets, supported by compelling empirical evidence (Table 3) and interpretable visualizations (Grad-CAM in Table 1)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 9 unlearning methods, 2 datasets, and multiple architectures with proper reporting of standard deviations from 3 independent trials
Systematic empirical analysis of metric hyperparameters, including calibration set size stability (Figure 1) and sensitivity to confidence level α across multiple settings
Well-executed ablation study (Figures 3-4) demonstrating distribution shifts in non-conformity scores with and without the proposed framework
weaknesses: Critical theoretical flaw: Footnote 1 acknowledges exchangeability—essential to conformal prediction's theoretical guarantees—'may not always hold in machine unlearning settings.' The paper applies conformal prediction without its theoretical foundation, undermining the core motivation

Incremental metric contributions: CR is simply Coverage/Set Size ratio, and MIACR is I(C(x)={0}). These are reasonable heuristics but lack conceptual novelty compared to existing uncertainty quantification approaches

Fundamental applicability limitation (Section B.4): Methods causing label corruption and distribution shifts (e.g., RL) require computationally expensive 'shadow models' for correction, revealing that metrics don't robustly handle all unlearning methods

Questionable conceptual premise: No clear argument that larger prediction sets for forget data indicate incomplete forgetting rather than expected uncertainty. Table 3 shows vastly different in-set ratios across methods (6%-100%), suggesting the problem is method-dependent, not universal

Weak ablation of proposed framework: No isolation of conformal prediction's contribution vs. C&W adversarial loss. Modest improvements (~3-5% UA, with TA decreases) could largely derive from adversarial training, not conformal prediction insights

Arbitrary hyperparameter choices: α default (0.1) lacks principled justification; calibration data requirement (2,000 CIFAR-10 samples) substantial and limits applicability; λ values (0, 0.2, 0.5, 1) selected arbitrarily with inconsistent evaluation criteria switching

Limited scope of framework evaluation: Applied to only 3 base methods (RT, FT, RL) of 9 evaluated; single task domain (image classification); trade-offs between forgetting quality and model utility incompletely characterized

Missing theoretical or empirical demonstration that CR/MIACR actually measure 'true forgetting' better—paper shows disagreement with UA but not that new metrics improve privacy guarantees or reflect genuine forgetting quality

strengths: Identifies a critical limitation in existing unlearning metrics through compelling empirical evidence (Table 3 shows 30-85% of misclassified data still appear in conformal prediction sets), revealing a genuine and important gap in evaluation methodology

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, Tiny ImageNet), models (ResNet-18, ViT), forgetting scenarios (random/class-wise), and 9 different unlearning methods, with proper reporting of standard deviations across 3 independent trials

Effective visualization and intuition for the core insight - Table 1's Grad-CAM analysis effectively demonstrates that excluding true labels from prediction sets leads to genuine forgetting (activation shifts away from object features)
Proposed metrics are practical and immediately applicable to evaluate existing unlearning methods without requiring modifications to base algorithms
Well-designed framework that improves forgetting quality while preserving predictive performance; consistent improvements across multiple methods and settings
Honest acknowledgment and discussion of limitations including exchangeability property violations, distribution shift handling, and hyperparameter sensitivity
weaknesses: Theoretical justification for conformal prediction application to machine unlearning is loose; CP is designed for test data uncertainty, not training data forgetting. The acknowledged caveat that 'exchangeability property may not always hold' substantially undermines the foundation. No justification for why CP is superior to other uncertainty quantification methods (Bayesian approaches, temperature scaling, etc.)

Metric design lacks principled justification: CR = Coverage/Set Size is a relatively simple combination without exploration of alternatives; MIACR's binary formulation is overly coarse; calibration set choices (2,000 samples, 50 per class) appear somewhat arbitrary despite stability analysis

Limited novelty of the proposed framework: C&W loss adaptation (Eq. 7→8) is straightforward replacement of probabilities with non-conformity scores; combining with original loss (Eq. 9) is standard practice without new insights into loss combination strategies

Distribution shift handling reveals metric limitations: Appendix B.4's 'shadow' and 'semi-shadow' models are post-hoc patches rather than principled solutions, suggesting CR struggles with label corruption and distribution-altering methods, limiting generalizability

Lacks statistical rigor: standard deviations reported but no significance tests (t-tests, confidence intervals provided); improvements are often modest (3-9% UA improvements, with some TA degradation) and statistical significance is unclear

Experimental concerns: FF method shows extreme degradation (UA 59.9%, RA 40.1%), either revealing incompatibility or raising fairness questions; FF omitted from Tiny ImageNet as 'computationally intractable' raises unaddressed scalability questions
Presentation could be more concise: dense tables (9, 10, 11, etc.) overwhelm readers; Q1-Q4 framing is somewhat contrived; key insights could be extracted more effectively from comprehensive results
Missing ablations on metric design: alternative CR formulations not explored; comparison to simpler baselines (e.g., Coverage alone) absent; sensitivity to calibration set distribution not analyzed

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: The empirical finding that 54.6% of UA-forgotten data still appears in conformal prediction sets (Table 2) raises legitimate concerns about metric reliability, effectively illustrated through Grad-CAM visualizations

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, Tiny ImageNet), architectures (ResNet-18, ViT), nine unlearning methods, and forgetting scenarios with extensive ablations and sensitivity analysis
Systematic metric design with clear logical construction: CR balances coverage and set size; MIACR applies stricter membership criterion; principled justification for improvements over UA/MIA
Practical framework demonstrating integration into existing methods with modest computational overhead (quantile-based threshold q̄)
Honest treatment of limitations including restricted scope (image classification), discussion of distribution-shift handling, and sensitivity analysis of hyperparameters (α, λ, calibration size)
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: Restriction to image classification substantially reduces impact; no experiments on language models, generation, or other domains where unlearning is increasingly important

Conceptual clarity issues: The term 'fake unlearning' conflates different notions of forgetting (conformal set membership vs. information leakage vs. privacy); for privacy-motivated unlearning, membership inference resistance is orthogonal to prediction set inclusion

Metrics lack theoretical grounding: CR is a straightforward ratio of conformal prediction quantities with no formal guarantees; MIACR's requirement C(x)={0} is extremely restrictive; no rigorous analysis connecting set membership to actual forgetting quality

Conformal prediction introduces practical dependencies: Requires separate calibration data; strong parameter sensitivity with α significantly affecting all results (Tables 7-12); α=0.05 recommendation not justified for unlearning context; shadow/semi-shadow models needed for distribution-shifted methods (Appendix B.5)

Limited technical novelty: CPU framework simply pushes S(x,y_t) > q̄ (straightforward C&W adaptation); specific to non-conformity score S(x,y)=1-p(x); margin Δ=0.01 unjustified; improvements modest (Table 5: UA 3.8%→7.9% with 1% TA drop)
Evaluation criteria ambiguity: 'Gap to RT' criterion questionable—RT is merely a baseline, not a principled target; unclear which of two criteria (①②) is preferable

Statistical and computational concerns: No significance tests despite large error bars; only 3 trials for reproducibility claims; computational costs of conformal inference and shadow models not quantified; scalability to large models unclear

Incomplete comparisons: No comparison to other uncertainty quantification methods (Bayesian, temperature scaling); limited discussion of alternatives; missing comparison to recent work on metric limitations
Distribution shift handling ad-hoc: Appendix B.5's shadow model approach lacks principled justification; complexity not clearly justified
Grad-CAM visualization is suggestive rather than rigorous evidence that label removal from prediction sets indicates better forgetting

strengths: Clear empirical identification of fake unlearning issue through conformal prediction recovery (~54% of misclassified data), well-documented with extensive evidence (Table 2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 9 unlearning methods, multiple scenarios, and datasets with thorough reporting of standard deviations and ablations
Intuitive visual motivation using Grad-CAM showing difference between methods that retain activation patterns vs. those that shift them when true labels leave prediction sets
Honest discussion of limitations regarding scope (image classification only), calibration data requirements, and other constraints
Well-organized presentation with extensive appendix providing multiple perspectives (various α values, class-wise forgetting, distribution shifts)
weaknesses: Fundamental conceptual issue: Paper conflates misclassification with forgetting. True label presence in conformal sets reflects model uncertainty, not necessarily incomplete forgetting. No formal justification that conformal set membership indicates genuine data traces remain

Weak connection between proposed metrics and privacy guarantees: CR and MIACR are based on conformal coverage, but paper never establishes correlation with actual privacy leakage under strong membership inference attacks. Critical gap between uncertainty quantification and forgetting verification

Severely limited experimental scope undermines generalization claims: Only image classification (CIFAR-10, Tiny ImageNet), no experiments on NLP/tabular/other domains, no comparison to alternative uncertainty methods (Bayesian, ensemble), only simple datasets/modest-scale models

Limited novelty of contributions: CR is merely Coverage/Set Size ratio (straightforward conformal prediction operation), MIACR simply checks if C(x)={0}, CPU framework minimally adapts C&W loss by replacing probability with threshold. 6.6% average UA improvement is modest

Heavy arbitrary design choices: α=0.05 chosen because 'standard' not application-justified; different α values substantially change conclusions (Tables 7-12); calibration data requirement dismissed too quickly despite being non-trivial in resource-constrained settings

Circular evaluation framework: Methods rank differently under two proposed criteria (CR vs MIACR) vs existing metrics (UA/MIA). Without ground truth forgetting benchmark, unclear which ranking is correct. No statistical significance testing despite reporting standard deviations

Fragility evident in distribution shift handling (Section B.5): Requiring 'shadow models' for methods like Random Label suggests approach is brittle and domain-sensitive, contradicting claimed generality

Unresolved gap between fake unlearning problem and solution: Paper identifies that UA/MIA miss true label presence in conformal sets, but doesn't rigorously establish this as privacy failure. Alternative explanation: these metrics measure misclassification, not forgetting—different goals

Missing critical experiments: No robustness to adaptive attacks on metrics, no formal privacy analysis (differential privacy bounds), no evaluation on large-scale models/datasets, no comparison to existing privacy-centric unlearning evaluation methods

Overstated contribution: Title claims 'Redefining Machine Unlearning' but work only proposes alternative metrics/minor framework tweak for narrow setting (image classification). Modest incremental contribution doesn't justify strong framing

strengths: Compelling identification and experimental validation of the 'fake unlearning' problem: convincingly demonstrates that 30-85% of misclassified forget data remain in conformal prediction sets, with strong visual evidence (Grad-CAM) and systematic empirical validation across 9 methods

Sound technical foundation: conformal prediction properly applied via split conformal prediction; creative integration of conformal thresholds into C&W loss formulation is well-motivated and mathematically rigorous

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 9 unlearning methods, 2 datasets, 2 architectures, multiple scenarios (random/class-wise forgetting), proper statistical reporting with standard deviations over 3 trials, thorough ablations on α and λ parameters

Proposed metrics are well-defined and grounded: CR and MIACR address real limitations of existing UA/MIA metrics by examining entire prediction sets rather than point predictions; Figures 7-10 convincingly show superiority
Clear presentation and structure: logical progression from problem identification to solution; good use of visualizations; honest discussion of limitations in Appendix D
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies established conformal prediction methods (Lei & Wasserman 2014) to unlearning; CPU framework is straightforward adaptation (Eq. 8→9) rather than fundamental innovation; no new unlearning algorithms proposed

Scope restricted to image classification: experiments only on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet; generalization to NLP, generative models, or other domains unexplored; significantly limits impact for a top-tier venue

Modest empirical improvements: average UA improvement 6.6% is useful but not substantial; CR improvements often modest (e.g., 0.864→0.763); high variance on Tiny ImageNet (e.g., NegGrad+ CRDf: 2.184±1.681) suggests instability

Insufficient metric design justification: CR = Coverage/Set Size lacks principled motivation—why this ratio over alternatives? Missing formal analysis of metric properties, scale invariance, sensitivity to number of classes. MIACR's strict requirement (C(x) = {0}) never justified as necessary for privacy preservation

Two evaluation criteria create ambiguity: 'Gap to RT' vs 'Limit-Based Criterion' frequently rank methods differently (Table 3); no principled guidance on which to prefer in different scenarios; weakens practical utility

Distribution shift handling incomplete and ad-hoc: shadow model approach (Section B.5) only in appendix, making main framework incomplete; complex implementation reduces reproducibility; unclear why main evaluation ignores this complication

Conformal prediction assumptions under adversarial training unexamined: CPU framework's adversarial loss is designed to push labels outside prediction sets—does this violate conformal prediction calibration guarantees? Not addressed theoretically or empirically

Reproducibility gaps: no code availability mentioned; parameter choices (Δ=0.01 'sufficient', calibration set >1000) lack justification; shadow models very difficult to reproduce from description alone

Missing critical comparisons: no comparison to alternative uncertainty quantification methods for unlearning evaluation; limited engagement with recent unlearning literature; no discussion of relationship to differential privacy notions
